INTRODUCTION 1.

This appeal has been filed under Order XLIII Rule 1 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI challenging an interim injunction order dated 10.08.2023 ("impugned order") passed by the Ld. ASCJ-cum-JSCC-cum-Guardian Judge, Dwarka Courts, New Delhi, in Suit No. CS-SCJ-1083/22.

sentences.text:
By virtue of the impugned order,
the trial court restrained Defendant No. 2 (Appellant herein) from:
a. Carrying out commercial or industrial activities in two alleged residential properties.

b. Parking large commercial vehicles and loading/unloading hazardous articles in the suit premises.
2.

The Appellant contends that:
a. One of the properties--Plot No. 77-A, Khasra No. 25/9, Block- H-1, Pole No. 5,
Pankaj Garden, Goela Dairy, Najafgarh, New Delhi--is not owned by her but by her Bhawana Kumari vs Saroj Devi on 22 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82130766/
1 husband (who is not impleaded).
b.

She holds valid licenses for the other premises she claims to own--Gali No. 1,
"87-A," Pankaj Garden, Goela Dairy, New Delhi.
c.
The impugned order effectively grants final relief at an interim stage.

3. The Plaintiff (Respondent) disputes these assertions, alleging that:
BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI a. The Appellant is misusing residential property for commercial purposes, in violation of municipal zoning laws. b. Any discrepancy in address is a ruse to evade liability, especially since MCD has initiated sealing proceedings under Section 345-A of the DMC Act against the premises identified as 77-A.
FACTUAL BACKGROUND 4.

The Plaintiff filed a suit for permanent and mandatory injunction, claiming that Defendant No. 2 was running commercial activities in two properties--(i) Gali No. 1, Pankaj Garden, Goela Dairy,
New Delhi (hereinafter "Property A"), and (ii) Plot No. 77-A, Khasra No. 25/9, Block-H-1, Pole No.
5, Pankaj Garden, Goela Dairy, Najafgarh, New Delhi (hereinafter "Property B").

Both properties,
according to the Plaintiff, lie in a residential zone under Delhi's Master Plan and municipal regulations.

5. The Plaintiff contends that the Defendant No. 2 stores "hazardous, dangerous, and highly inflammable articles" and regularly brings in large commercial vehicles, causing public nuisance and safety hazards for residents.

6. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), arrayed as Defendant No. 1, submitted in its status report that sealing action was initiated under Section 345-A of the Delhi Municipal Corporation BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI (DMC) Act in respect of "Plot No. 77-A" due to non-conforming commercial activity.

sentences.text: 7. The trial court, having considered the Plaintiff's complaints, the MCD's report, and the mismatch in addresses claimed by the Appellant, concluded that the Plaintiff had shown a prima facie case of unauthorized commercial use.
It also found that balance of convenience and irreparable harm weighed in the Plaintiff's favor, prompting the interim injunction.
APPELLANT'S CONTENTIONS 8.

The contentions on behalf of the Appellant are as follows:
a.
The Appellant states that Property B (77-A) belongs to her husband, who is not a party to the suit, and hence any injunction against her in relation to that property is misdirected.
b. The Appellant claims ownership only over "87-A," for which she holds a General Trade/Storage License valid until 31.03.2024.

She also references a Food Bhawana Kumari vs Saroj Devi on 22 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82130766/

license (FSSAI) for "Plot No. 162," a different location, insisting she has legal authority to store FMCG goods.

c. It is argued that the impugned order essentially shuts down her trade and livelihood,
contravening the principle that interim relief should be merely preventive, not determinative.
BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI PLAINTIFF'S (RESPONDENT'S) CONTENTIONS 9.

sentences.text:
The contentions on behalf of the Plaintiff/Respondent are as follows:
a.

The Plaintiff avers that residential zoning bars commercial or industrial activity,
especially storage of hazardous goods.
The MCD's sealing action at "77-A" supports the Plaintiff's stance that unauthorized business operations are ongoing.
b. The Plaintiff alleges that any confusion over addresses (77-A vs. 87-A) is orchestrated to evade legal consequences.
Further, no license specifically authorizes the Appellant to operate a commercial enterprise in either "77-A" or "87-A" if they remain zoned residential.
c. The Plaintiff emphasizes the nuisance caused by heavy vehicles blocking roads, as well as the risk posed by inflammable materials stored in close proximity to residential dwellings.
POINTS FOR DETERMINATION 10.

From the above, the key issues for consideration are:
a. Whether the trial court erred in finding a prima facie case of unauthorized commercial use, given the disputes over property addresses and ownership.
BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI b.
Whether the licenses produced by the Appellant (General Trade/Storage and Food Safety) sufficiently justify commercial activity in a purported residential area.
c. Whether the balance of convenience and potential irreparable harm favor maintaining or vacating the injunction.
d. Whether the impugned order amounts to granting final relief at the interim stage.
DISCUSSION AND FINDINGS Prima Facie Case in Light of Zoning and Sealing Action 11.
Under the Master Plan of Delhi (MPD) and relevant municipal bye-laws, areas designated as residential are subject to stringent restrictions on any commercial or industrial use.
Such restrictions are intended to safeguard the peaceful character of residential neighborhoods and protect residents from noise, traffic congestion, and potential safety hazards.

When a property in a residential zone is allegedly used for non-residential purposes without due approval or conversion, it ordinarily raises a strong presumption of illegality unless the occupant can prove lawful mixed-use Bhawana Kumari vs Saroj Devi on 22 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82130766/
3 or commercial authorization.

12. In the instant case, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has initiated sealing proceedings under Section 345-A of the Delhi Municipal Corporation (DMC) Act against one of the suit BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI properties (i.e., Plot No. 77-A).

entities.text: BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI properties
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Section 345-A empowers the MCD to seal premises that are being misused in violation of permissible land- use rules.
The very fact that MCD--a statutory authority--has found enough material to invoke sealing provisions lends substantive weight to the allegation of non-conforming usage.
While such action is not conclusive proof of illegality, it forms a credible official stance that the property is being employed in a manner inconsistent with its residential classification.
13. The Appellant denies ownership of the property flagged by MCD (77-A) and asserts instead that she owns "87-A."

Even if the Appellant's disclaimers are eventually borne out at trial, the core inquiry at the interim stage remains whether unauthorized commercial activity is taking place, not strictly who holds title.
A defendant in control or effective possession--whether as owner, tenant, or agent-- can be enjoined if the property is being used in a manner violating municipal regulations.

Consequently, the Appellant's disclaimer of ownership does not by itself negate the prima facie evidence arising from MCD's sealing action; rather, it underscores a factual dispute that will be resolved at trial.
14. The Plaintiff's complaint, fortified by MCD's official records of sealing, plausibly indicates that the property (77-A) is subject to non-residential use in a residential neighborhood.

Equally relevant is the mismatch in address references (77-A vs. 87-A vs. BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI other addresses) and the Appellant's own admission of conducting business operations under a general trade license.
Even if the Appellant has some form of trade/storage license, such a license typically does not override the underlying land-use classification.
Unless it is shown that the premises have been legally converted or recognized for commercial purposes, the occupant's activities likely remain prima facie unauthorized under municipal law.

15. At the interim stage, the court is tasked with assessing whether there is sufficient reason to believe that unlawful commercial usage is taking place in a residential zone--not to conclusively determine the property's true owner or the final legality of every license.
MCD's decision to invoke Section 345-A of the DMC Act is a substantial indicator that the premises are not being used in conformity with applicable zoning norms.

Therefore, the combination of (i) a statutory authority's sealing action, (ii) clear zoning prohibitions under MPD, and (iii) the occupant's admissions of operating a commercial trade collectively establish a strong prima facie case of non-conforming use pending final adjudication of factual disputes such as correct addresses and actual ownership.

Effect and Scope of Licenses 19. A license for general trade or storage, issued by the municipal corporation, primarily attests that the licensee has complied with certain administrative prerequisites--such as paying requisite BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI fees, meeting basic safety or hygiene requirements, and declaring the intended nature of goods to be stored or sold.

Such a license, however, does not Bhawana Kumari vs Saroj Devi on 22 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82130766/
4 override the fundamental land-use classification of the property under the Master Plan or municipal bye-laws.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Even if the occupant holds a valid general trade/storage license, it remains incumbent on them to show that the premises are lawfully zoned or converted for the licensed commercial activity.

20. In the instant case, the Appellant has produced two main licenses:
a. A General Trade/Storage License purportedly covering "Property No. 87-A, Gali No. 1," valid only until a specified date (e.g., 31.03.2024).
b. A Food Safety (FSSAI) License for "Plot No. 162, Khasra No. 25/2/4," which is neither 77-A nor 87-A.
21.

These inconsistencies in addresses raise the question of whether the licensed property is the same as the suit property and whether the license actually extends to the exact premises alleged to be misused.
Unless it is shown that the address on the license matches the property being used commercially, the license's protective ambit may not apply.
22. While a trade/storage license authorizes the licensee to conduct certain specified activities, it does not confer authority to BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI breach zoning restrictions.

For instance, a license to store FMCG goods or run a small-scale trade does not itself legalize the presence of commercial activity in a zone strictly designated for residential use unless the property has been lawfully converted or falls under a permissible mixed-use policy.
Consequently, a license must be read in conjunction with land-use approvals--if the latter are absent, the license cannot legalize an otherwise unauthorized commercial venture.

23. At this interim stage, the trial court is not required to definitively rule on whether the license fully legalizes the occupant's activities; rather, it must assess whether the occupant's reliance on such a license adequately counters the Plaintiff's allegations of zoning violation.
The discrepancies in addresses coupled with the strict nature of residential zoning laws suggest that the licenses alone do not refute the prima facie case of unauthorized commercial use.

Whether the license indeed covers the suit property or whether the property has been officially converted for commercial activity can only be settled upon full trial and production of conclusive evidence.
24. Ultimately, these licenses may be relevant to operational or safety standards, but they do not, in themselves, confer immunity from allegations of non-conforming land use.

The mismatch of addresses, the restricted scope of trade/storage permissions, and the absence of clear evidence that the property is validly zoned for BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI commercial activity collectively indicate that the licenses presented by the Appellant do not, at this stage, negate the Plaintiff's contention of illegal commercial use in a residential area.
Balance of Convenience and Irreparable Harm 25.
The alleged storage of inflammable/hazardous materials and the use of large vehicles in a residential colony pose significant risks.

If the Plaintiff's apprehensions are valid, maintaining status Bhawana Kumari vs Saroj Devi on 22 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82130766/
5 quo by restraining such use prevents potential irreparable harm to the neighborhood.
26. While the Appellant may face business disruptions, any commercial activity must comply with municipal and zoning laws.
Should the Appellant eventually establish legitimate entitlement to conduct trade at the premises, she may seek appropriate redress or dissolution of the injunction.
The balance of convenience thus weighs in favor of protecting residential dwellers and ensuring compliance with land-use regulations.
Interim Injunction vs. Final Relief 27.
A temporary injunction aims to preserve status quo and protect the Plaintiff from continuing harm during the litigation.
The trial court has not granted a decree in the Plaintiff's favor; it has merely restrained commercial activities that are prima facie unlawful.
BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI 28.

Hon'ble Supreme Court in Wander Ltd. v. Antox India Pvt. Ltd., 1990 (Supp) SCC 727, held that an appellate court will not readily interfere unless the trial court's discretion is exercised arbitrarily or capriciously.

entities.text: Wander Ltd. v. Antox India Pvt. Ltd., 1990 (Supp) SCC 727
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Here, the order arises from documented MCD findings and a reasoned application of the three-fold test (prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable harm).
Therefore, no arbitrariness is apparent.
CONCLUSION 29.
On the basis of the above discussion, this Court finds no merit in the appeal.
The trial court correctly applied the relevant legal tests and considered the conflicting factual scenarios relating to ownership, address, and licensing.
The unresolved disputes-- including whether the Appellant's husband is the actual owner of "77- A" or whether "87-A" is validly licensed for commercial use--are fit for final adjudication upon trial.
30. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the impugned order dated 10.08.2023 is hereby upheld.

It is clarified that the trial court's injunction does not amount to final determination of the parties' rights; it merely safeguards the alleged residential locality from potential hazards and nuisance.
BHAWNA KUMARI VS SAROJ DEVI 31.
Nothing in this order shall be construed as an opinion on the suit's ultimate merits.
A copy of this judgment, along with the lower court record, be sent to the trial court for further proceedings.
32. The Ahlmad is directed to send a certified copy of this judgment to the Ld. Trial Court along with the record of the Ld. Trial Court.
Also, the Ahlmad of this Court is directed to consign the appeal file to the record room, after completion of necessary formalities.
